steps.name: prompt
steps.text: Write the introduction for our paper on CENAS, a multi-objective evolutionary NAS method that uses a Pareto-wise ranking classifier instead of a performance predictor. Cover the background on NAS and multi-objective ENAS, the rank disorder problem with regression predictors, our idea and method, and the contributions and paper outline.

steps.name: detailed_outline
steps.text:
- NAS background
  - automates design of task-specific network architectures vs hand-crafted DNNs needing human expertise
  - matches human-expert architectures, also finds new state-of-the-art ones
  - since Google Brain's NAS: two stages
  - early stage: training-from-scratch (NASNet, NAS-RL); time-consuming, expensive; NASNet 32400-43200 GPU hours on CIFAR-10
  - current stage: one-shot NAS with weight sharing; params inherited from supernet; only train supernet -> faster evaluation
  - Sinha et al.: improved weight sharing with new decoding of architecture parameters, more gradient info to given architectures, better predictive capability
  - categories: EA-based, RL-based, gradient-based, Bayesian-based, local/random search-based
- Multi-objective view
  - conflicting objectives (accuracy, FLOPs, energy, latency) + expensive architecture evaluation
  - many evolutionary algorithms NAS (ENAS) methods
  - Lu et al.: NSGANetV1, classification performance vs FLOPs; Bayesian models + downsampling architectures for efficiency
  - Dudziak et al.: hardware-aware, latency vs accuracy, latency replaced by GCN-based latency predictor
  - vs RL and gradient methods: ENAS needs no gradient info, insensitive to discontinuity / non-differentiability
- Predictors and rank disorder
  - popular: performance predictors to save evaluation cost
  - PRE-NAS: few representative architectures as training samples for online accuracy predictor, evaluated by high-fidelity weight inheritance; effectiveness shown in extended PRE-NAS work
  - typical procedure: (1) train high-accurate surrogate (e.g., regression) on well-trained architectures; (2) predict accuracy value; (3) choose optima by numerical values of multiple objectives
  - rank disorder: good architecture ranked poorly vs worse one
  - reason (1): fitting loss (e.g. MSE); A = 0.8, B = 0.9 true; squared residuals -> predicted 0.85 for A, 0.84 for B; A chosen, B better; search misled
  - reason (2): limited compute / expensive evaluation; accurate regression hard with few samples; Pareto dominance ineffective, especially with more objectives
- Our idea
  - inspired by ordinal optimization theory: qualitatively decide good or not, not quantitative comparison of predicted values / indicators
  - matches end-to-end nature of ENAS: goal = select promising architectures for next-round evolution in environmental selection
- CENAS
  - Comparator-based Pareto Evolution for NAS; online Pareto-wise end-to-end ranking classifier
  - predicts dominance relation between candidate and reference architectures (chosen by adaptive clustering)
  - good class: dominate or non-dominated with references; poor: dominated
  - \alpha -dominance evaluation against class imbalance, regulates good/poor rate
- Contributions
  - 1. Pareto-wise ranking classifier: multi-objective NAS -> Pareto-dominance classification; ordinal optimization alleviates rank disorder in environmental selection; first attempt
  - 2. classifier-based Pareto evolution framework; two adaptive schemes: reference selection, \alpha -dominance for class imbalance
  - 3. experiments on widely-used datasets, cutting-edge results (esp. search efficiency); Photovoltaic cell, best-known results
- Organization: II motivation, III CENAS, IV experiments, V conclusions

steps.name: partial_draft
steps.text:
Neural architecture search (NAS) is known as an effective way to automate the design of neural network architectures for specific tasks, instead of designing hand-crafted DNNs that need a lot of human expertise. It has been shown that NAS can not only get DNN architectures that are competitive with what human experts design, but can also find new state-of-the-art architectures.

Since Google Brain's NAS, NAS development has gone through two stages. In the early stage NAS was based on training-from-scratch, for example NASNet and NAS-RL. But these methods are time-consuming and computationally expensive. For example, NASNet needs 32400-43200 GPU hours to train on a common dataset like CIFAR-10. In the current stage, one-shot NAS methods based on weight sharing are popular. This means that the parameters of the candidate architectures are inherited directly from a supernet. So we only have to train the supernet, and the performance evaluation can be sped up a lot,. For example, Sinha et al. improved the weight sharing approach with a new decoding technique for the architecture parameters, which can divert more gradient information to the given architectures, and in this way the predictive capability of the given architectures is improved. Overall, existing NAS approaches can roughly be divided into EA-based, RL-based, gradient-based, Bayesian-based, and local/random search-based classes.

From the multi-objective optimization point of view, NAS is a complex multi-objective optimization problem, which has multiple conflicting objectives (e.g., accuracy, FLOPs, energy, and latency) and architecture evaluation that is computationally expensive. A variety of evolutionary algorithms NAS (ENAS) methods have been developed to solve multi-objective NAS. For example, Lu et al. presented NSGANetV1, which is one of the most representative multi-objective methods for optimizing CNN architectures, and it takes classification performance and FLOPs as two conflicting objectives. In that study they used Bayesian models and downsampling architectures to improve computational efficiency. Also, Dudziak et al. tried to find hardware-aware architectures by optimizing two objectives (i.e., latency and accuracy), and the latency is replaced by a latency predictor based on a graph convolutional network (GCN). Compared to methods driven by conventional reinforcement learning (RL) and gradient algorithms, EA-based NAS (ENAS) methods do not need gradient information of the objectives and they are insensitive to discontinuity and non-differentiability of the objectives.

A popular way in existing ENAS methods is to use performance predictors to predict the performance value of every candidate, which saves a lot of the expensive cost of architecture evaluation. For example, PRE-NAS selected a small number of representative architectures as training samples for an online accuracy predictor, and the representative architectures were evaluated by high-fidelity weight inheritance during the evolutionary search. The extended work of PRE-NAS fully demonstrated how effective this strategy is. Typically these methods follow the same procedure: (1) train a highly accurate surrogate (e.g., regression model) on a set of well-trained architectures; (2) predict the numerical value of the accuracy of a candidate architecture; and (3) decide the optimal solutions based on the numerical values of the multiple objectives. But this procedure easily suffers from the rank disorder issue, where a high-performance candidate architecture can get a poor ranking compared with a worse architecture according to the trained predictor. There are two reasons for this.

- reason (1): surrogate fitting loss (e.g. MSE); A true 0.8, B true 0.9; squared residuals -> predicted 0.85 A, 0.84 B; A selected though B better; search misled by mispredicted low-accuracy solutions
- reason (2): limited compute / expensive evaluation; accurate regression hard with limited samples; Pareto dominance becomes ineffective, esp. as number of objectives grows
- Our idea: inspired by ordinal optimization theory; qualitative good/not good instead of quantitative comparison; fits end-to-end nature of ENAS (select promising architectures for next-round evolution)
- CENAS: online Pareto-wise end-to-end ranking classifier; dominance relation between candidate and reference architectures (adaptive clustering); good = dominate or non-dominated, poor = dominated; \alpha -dominance evaluation for class imbalance
- Contributions: 1. classifier turns multi-objective NAS into Pareto-dominance classification, alleviates rank disorder, first attempt; 2. classifier-based Pareto evolution framework + two adaptive schemes; 3. experiments on widely-used datasets, cutting-edge results (esp. search efficiency), Photovoltaic cell best-known results
- Organization: II motivation, III CENAS, IV experiments, V conclusions

steps.name: rough_draft
steps.text:
Neural architecture search (NAS) is known as an effective way to automate the design of neural network architectures for specific tasks, instead of designing hand-crafted DNNs that need a lot of human expertise. It has been shown that NAS can not only get DNN architectures that are competitive with what human experts design, but can also find new state-of-the-art architectures.

Since Google Brain's NAS, NAS development has gone through two stages. In the early stage NAS was based on training-from-scratch, for example NASNet and NAS-RL. But these methods are time-consuming and computationally expensive. For example, NASNet needs 32400-43200 GPU hours to train on a common dataset like CIFAR-10. In the current stage, one-shot NAS methods based on weight sharing are popular. This means that the parameters of the candidate architectures are inherited directly from a supernet. So we only have to train the supernet, and the performance evaluation can be sped up a lot,. For example, Sinha et al. improved the weight sharing approach with a new decoding technique for the architecture parameters, which can divert more gradient information to the given architectures, and in this way the predictive capability of the given architectures is improved. Overall, existing NAS approaches can roughly be divided into EA-based, RL-based, gradient-based, Bayesian-based, and local/random search-based classes.

From the multi-objective optimization point of view, NAS is a complex multi-objective optimization problem, which has multiple conflicting objectives (e.g., accuracy, FLOPs, energy, and latency) and architecture evaluation that is computationally expensive. A variety of evolutionary algorithms NAS (ENAS) methods have been developed to solve multi-objective NAS. For example, Lu et al. presented NSGANetV1, which is one of the most representative multi-objective methods for optimizing CNN architectures, and it takes classification performance and FLOPs as two conflicting objectives. In that study they used Bayesian models and downsampling architectures to improve computational efficiency. Also, Dudziak et al. tried to find hardware-aware architectures by optimizing two objectives (i.e., latency and accuracy), and the latency is replaced by a latency predictor based on a graph convolutional network (GCN). Compared to methods driven by conventional reinforcement learning (RL) and gradient algorithms, EA-based NAS (ENAS) methods do not need gradient information of the objectives and they are insensitive to discontinuity and non-differentiability of the objectives.

A popular way in existing ENAS methods is to use performance predictors to predict the performance value of every candidate, which saves a lot of the expensive cost of architecture evaluation. For example, PRE-NAS selected a small number of representative architectures as training samples for an online accuracy predictor, and the representative architectures were evaluated by high-fidelity weight inheritance during the evolutionary search. The extended work of PRE-NAS fully demonstrated how effective this strategy is. Typically these methods follow the same procedure: (1) train a highly accurate surrogate (e.g., regression model) on a set of well-trained architectures; (2) predict the numerical value of the accuracy of a candidate architecture; and (3) decide the optimal solutions based on the numerical values of the multiple objectives. But this procedure easily suffers from the rank disorder issue, where a high-performance candidate architecture can get a poor ranking compared with a worse architecture according to the trained predictor. There are two reasons for this.

(1) A surrogate model that fits a loss function (e.g. MSE) can easily lead to the rank disorder issue. Take MSE as an example and compare two architectures A and B, whose ground-truth accuracy is 0.8 and 0.9. Because of the squared residuals, the model may give a reasonable result where the predicted accuracy is 0.85 for A and 0.84 for B. Then A, which has the higher predicted accuracy, will be selected even though B is better in practice. So the search can be misled by solutions that have low accuracy but are mispredicted to have high accuracy.

(2) Limited computing resources or expensive evaluations make the rank disorder issue even worse during the architecture search. This is because it is hard to get a highly accurate regression model with limited training samples, so inaccurate performance evaluations happen and make the rank disorder issue worse. Once rank disorder happens, the Pareto dominance relationship tends to become ineffective, especially when the number of objectives increases.

To alleviate the rank disorder issue and build a robust surrogate model with limited computing resources, we take inspiration from ordinal optimization theory and come up with an idea: only qualitatively determine whether architectures are good or not, instead of comparing them quantitatively with predicted objective values or performance indicators. Actually our idea fits the end-to-end nature of ENAS. That is, the essential goal of the search in ENAS is to select a number of promising architectures with good performance for the next round of evolution during environmental selection.

So we propose a Comparator-based Pareto Evolution approach for NAS (CENAS), where an online Pareto-wise end-to-end ranking classifier is learned to recognize optimal architectures in the multi-objective search. The classifier can predict the dominance relationship between a candidate architecture and reference architectures, which are selected by an adaptive clustering method. In other words, candidate architectures are classified into a good class and a poor class, where good architectures either dominate the reference ones or are non-dominated with them, and poor ones are dominated by the references. To avoid the class imbalance problem we design an \alpha -dominance evaluation method that improves classification accuracy by regulating the rate between candidate architectures in the good class and the poor class.

The main contributions of this paper are:

- 1. We design the Pareto-wise end-to-end ranking classifier to turn a complex multi-objective NAS task into a simple Pareto-dominance classification task. This classifier, based on ordinal optimization, can effectively alleviate the rank disorder problem in environmental selection. This is the first attempt to use the Pareto dominance classification concept to simplify the NAS search process.

- 2. We devise the classifier-based Pareto evolution framework to make NAS more efficient and effective. We also design two adaptive schemes to make sure the classifier is reliable during the evolutionary process. One selects reference architectures for the classification, and the other eliminates the class imbalance issue with \alpha -dominance evaluation.

- 3. The experimental results show the practicality and scalability of the proposed framework on multiple widely-used datasets, and it achieves cutting-edge results in various critical performance metrics (especially search efficiency). We also show the performance of the proposed method on Photovoltaic cell, where it achieves the best-known results.

The rest of this paper is organized as follows. Section II presents the motivation. Section III describes CENAS in detail. Section IV presents the experimental settings and comparative results between CENAS and other state-of-the-art approaches. Section V gives the conclusions and future directions.

steps.text:
Neural architecture search (NAS) is known as an effective way to automate the design of task-specific neural network architectures, instead of designing hand-crafted DNNs based on extensive human expertise [1,2,3,4]. It has been demonstrated that NAS can not only achieve DNN architectures competitive with those of human experts, but also discover new state-of-the-art architectures [3,4].

Starting from Google Brain’s NAS [5], the development of NAS has gone through two stages [6]. The early stage saw NAS based on training-from-scratch [7,8,9,10], such as NASNet [11] and NAS-RL [5]. These methods are, however, time-consuming and computationally expensive [12]. For example, NASNet [11] consumes 32400-43200 GPU hours for training on a common dataset like CIFAR-10. In the current stage, one-shot NAS methods based on weight sharing [4,13,14,15,16,17] are prevalent: the parameters of candidate architectures are directly inherited from a supernet, so that only the supernet needs to be trained and performance evaluation can be significantly sped up [18], [19]. For example, Sinha et al. [20] improved the weight sharing approach with a new decoding technique for the architecture parameters, which diverts more gradient information to the given architectures and thereby enhances their predictive capability. Overall, existing NAS approaches can be roughly divided into EA-based [21], RL-based [22], gradient-based [15], Bayesian-based [23,24], and local/random search-based [17] classes.

From the perspective of multi-objective optimization, NAS is a complex problem involving multiple conflicting objectives (e.g., accuracy, FLOPs, energy, and latency) [13,18,5] and computationally expensive architecture evaluation [14,18,25]. To solve multi-objective NAS, a variety of evolutionary algorithms NAS (ENAS) methods have been developed [26,27,28,29]. For example, Lu et al. [29] presented NSGANetV1, one of the most representative multi-objective methods for optimizing CNN architectures, which takes classification performance and FLOPs as two conflicting objectives and uses Bayesian models and downsampling architectures to improve computational efficiency. In addition, Dudziak et al. [30] aimed to find hardware-aware architectures by optimizing latency and accuracy, where the latency is replaced by a graph convolutional network (GCN) based latency predictor. In contrast to methods driven by conventional reinforcement learning (RL) [13,5] and gradient algorithms [15,31], EA-based NAS (ENAS) methods [32,26,27,21] are free from the gradient information of the objectives and insensitive to their discontinuity and non-differentiability [33,5,11,34].

A popular approach in existing ENAS methods is to use performance predictors to predict the performance of each candidate, which largely saves the expensive cost of architecture evaluation. For example, PRE-NAS [35] selected a small number of representative architectures as training samples for an online accuracy predictor, where these architectures were evaluated by high-fidelity weight inheritance during the evolutionary search. The effectiveness of this strategy has been fully demonstrated in the extended work of PRE-NAS [36]. Typically, these methods follow the same procedure: (1) train a highly accurate surrogate (e.g., regression model) on a set of well-trained architectures; (2) predict the numerical accuracy of a candidate architecture; and (3) determine the optimal solutions according to the numerical values of multiple objectives. However, this procedure easily suffers from the rank disorder issue [3], in which a high-performance candidate architecture may be ranked below a worse architecture by the trained predictor. The reasons are as follows.

(1) A surrogate model fitting a loss function (e.g. MSE) may easily lead to the rank disorder issue [18,25]. Taking MSE as an example, consider two architectures A and B whose ground-truth accuracies are 0.8 and 0.9, respectively. Due to the squared residuals [3], the model may give a reasonable result in which the predicted accuracy is 0.85 for A and 0.84 for B. Thus A, with the higher predicted accuracy, will be selected even though B is better in practice. Consequently, the search can be misled by low-accuracy solutions that are mispredicted as high-accuracy ones.

(2) Limited computing resources or expensive evaluations make the rank disorder issue even worse during the architecture search [15,37]. This is because a highly accurate regression model is difficult to obtain with limited training samples, so inaccurate performance evaluations further deteriorate the rank disorder issue. Once rank disorder occurs, the Pareto dominance relationship tends to be ineffective, especially as the number of objectives increases [18] [38].

To alleviate the rank disorder issue and build a robust surrogate model under limited computing resources, we are inspired by ordinal optimization theory [39] and propose an idea: only qualitatively determine whether architectures are good or not, instead of quantitatively comparing them with predicted objective values or performance indicators. In fact, this idea accords with the end-to-end nature of ENAS, whose essential goal during environmental selection is to select a number of promising architectures with good performance for the next round of evolution.

Accordingly, we propose a Comparator-based Pareto Evolution approach for NAS (CENAS), where an online Pareto-wise end-to-end ranking classifier is learnt to recognize optimal architectures in the multi-objective search. The classifier predicts the dominance relationship between a candidate architecture and reference architectures selected by an adaptive clustering method. In other words, candidate architectures are classified into good and poor classes: good architectures either dominate or are non-dominated with the reference ones, while poor ones are dominated by the references. To avoid the class imbalance problem, we design an \alpha -dominance evaluation method that enhances classification accuracy by regulating the rate between candidate architectures in the good and poor classes.

The main contributions of this paper include:

- 1. The Pareto-wise end-to-end ranking classifier is designed to transform a complex multi-objective NAS task into a simple Pareto-dominance classification task. This ordinal optimization-based classifier can effectively alleviate the rank disorder problem in environmental selection. This is the first attempt to use the Pareto dominance classification concept to simplify the search process of NAS.

- 2. The classifier-based Pareto evolution framework is devised to enhance the efficiency and effectiveness of NAS. In addition, two adaptive schemes are designed to ensure the reliability of the classifier during the evolutionary process: one selects reference architectures for the classification, and the other eliminates the class imbalance issue by \alpha -dominance evaluation.

- 3. The experimental results demonstrate the practicality and scalability of the proposed framework on multiple widely-used datasets, achieving cutting-edge results in various critical performance metrics (especially search efficiency). Besides, we show the performance of the proposed method on Photovoltaic cell, where it achieves the best-known results.

The rest of this paper is organized as follows. Section II presents the motivation. Section III details the proposed CENAS. Section IV presents the experimental settings and comparative results between CENAS and other state-of-the-art approaches. Finally, Section V draws the conclusions and future directions.
